meenakshi-amman-temple.hook: The living heart of a 2,500-year-old city
meenakshi-amman-temple.why: Few places on earth have been worshipped, rebuilt and celebrated without a break for as long as this one. Madurai grew around Meenakshi in concentric squares, so every street you walk eventually leads back to her gopurams. Inside, thousands of painted figures crowd the towers, pilgrims circle the Golden Lotus tank as they have for centuries, and at night the temple puts Shiva to bed with music, lamps and a palanquin procession.
see: The 14 gopurams, the tallest on the south side, covered in painted figures
The Golden Lotus tank (Porthamarai Kulam), where poets were once judged
The Hall of a Thousand Pillars and its temple art museum
The night Palliarai ceremony, around 9–9:30 pm
meenakshi-amman-temple.best: 5–7 am for quiet darshan, or 8:30 pm for the night ceremony
meenakshi-amman-temple.know: Phones are not allowed inside; use the counters at the gates. Dress modestly: shoulders and knees covered.

koodal-azhagar-temple.hook: Vishnu on three floors, five minutes from Meenakshi
koodal-azhagar-temple.why: One of the 108 Divya Desams sacred to Vishnu, and one of the few where you can see him in three postures stacked one above another: seated, standing and reclining. Climb the inner stairs of the tower and the city's rooftops open up around you. It is calm, beautifully carved and almost always less crowded than Meenakshi.
see: The three-tiered shrine: Vishnu seated, standing and reclining
Carved pillars of the main mandapam
The view from the tower stairs

immaiyil-nanmai-tharuvar-temple.hook: The rare shrine where Shiva himself worships
immaiyil-nanmai-tharuvar-temple.why: Most temples show gods being worshipped. Here, Shiva is shown worshipping the lingam, a story that makes this small, ancient temple special to Madurai's devotees. It is one of the city's five-element shrines (the earth temple), tucked into the Periyar area and easy to add to any old-city walk.
see: The image of Shiva in worship
The old stone mandapams away from the crowds

thiruvappudaiyar-temple.hook: A temple the Tamil saints sang about
thiruvappudaiyar-temple.why: Praised in the Devaram hymns more than a thousand years ago, this Shiva temple on the north bank of the Vaigai is a quiet counterpoint to the old city. Locals come for the calm; travellers come for a glimpse of everyday temple life away from the tour groups.
see: Sellur's lanes and butter-bun stalls nearby

vandiyur-mariamman-teppakulam.hook: A royal tank built on the scale of a lake
vandiyur-mariamman-teppakulam.why: Thirumalai Nayak built this enormous square tank in the 17th century, with a pavilion on an island in the middle. Most of the year it is a place where families stroll at sunset and snack carts gather. Once a year, in the Tamil month of Thai, Meenakshi and Sundareswarar are floated across it on a lamp-lit raft in one of Madurai's loveliest festivals.
see: The island mandapam and its garden
The float festival (Thai full moon, Jan–Feb)
vandiyur-mariamman-teppakulam.best: Late afternoon to evening; Jan–Feb for the float festival

pandi-muneeswarar-temple.hook: Where Madurai brings its prayers for justice
pandi-muneeswarar-temple.why: Pandi Kovil is a folk temple, loud and joyful, and nothing like the grand stone temples. Tradition says its deity is the Pandya king Nedunchezhiyan, the king of the Silappathikaram epic, who chose to be buried here as penance. Families come to cook pongal, tie bells, make vows and ask for protection. Visit to see how faith is lived in Madurai, not just admired.
see: Pongal cooked in the open as an offering
The vow bells and the guardian shrines
Independence Day's communal feast for thousands (15 August)
pandi-muneeswarar-temple.best: Mornings, when families come to cook pongal
pandi-muneeswarar-temple.know: A working folk temple: some families offer animal sacrifice at the subsidiary shrine.

thiruparankundram-murugan-temple.hook: Murugan's first abode, carved into a sacred hill
thiruparankundram-murugan-temple.why: Of the six great abodes of Murugan, this is the first, and the place where he married Deivanai. The temple is cut into the living rock of the hill, so the sanctum feels like a cave of light and stone. Above it rises the bare granite hill itself, with a hilltop dargah, and at its foot the Saravana Poigai tank. It is one of the most atmospheric places of worship in South India.
see: The rock-cut sanctum with Murugan and Deivanai
The climb up the hill for views over Madurai
Kanda Sashti in Oct–Nov, the temple's greatest festival
thiruparankundram-murugan-temple.best: Early morning, before the heat on the rock

yoga-narasimha-temple-yanaimalai.hook: A cave temple inside Elephant Hill
yoga-narasimha-temple-yanaimalai.why: Yanaimalai looks like a giant elephant lying down on the plain, and in its side is a rock-cut cave temple to Narasimha in meditation, carved in 770 CE. The same hill holds ancient Jain beds. Arrive late in the afternoon and stay for the sunset across the paddy fields.
see: The rock-cut Yoga Narasimha shrine (770 CE)
The elephant shape of the hill from the road

kalamegha-perumal-temple-thirumohur.hook: Vishnu's temple of the ancient Tamil classics
kalamegha-perumal-temple-thirumohur.why: A Divya Desam of Vishnu in a village east of Madurai, with a large temple tank and a much-loved shrine of Chakrathazhwar, the god's divine discus in human form. It is unhurried, rural and rich in carving: an easy add-on to Yanaimalai.
see: Village life around the temple car streets

kallazhagar-temple-alagar-kovil.hook: Meenakshi's brother, in a temple at the forest's edge
kallazhagar-temple-alagar-kovil.why: At the foot of the green Alagar hills, Vishnu is worshipped as Kallazhagar, Meenakshi's brother. Every Chithirai he travels in procession to Madurai and enters the Vaigai on a golden horse while the whole city turns out to greet him. The temple itself is grand and old, with fortified walls, and the road up through the forest leads to Pazhamudircholai.
see: The great gopuram and fort walls
The Pathinettam Padi Karuppasamy shrine at the gate
Monkeys and forest on the hill road
kallazhagar-temple-alagar-kovil.best: Morning; carry water and keep food away from the monkeys
kallazhagar-temple-alagar-kovil.spend: 1.5 hours, half a day with Pazhamudircholai

pazhamudircholai-murugan-temple.hook: Murugan's sixth abode, high in the forest
pazhamudircholai-murugan-temple.why: The road climbs through thick forest above Alagar Kovil to the last of Murugan's six abodes. This is where, the story goes, a boy under a jamun tree asked the poet Avvaiyar whether she wanted her fruit hot or cold, and taught the wise old woman a lesson. Cooler air, birdsong and a small, colourful temple make it feel a world away from the city.
see: The temple and its jamun-tree legend

thirumalai-nayakkar-mahal.hook: A king's palace of giant pillars
thirumalai-nayakkar-mahal.why: Built in 1636 by Thirumalai Nayak, this palace mixes Dravidian and Islamic styles on a scale that still stuns: a vast courtyard ringed by massive white pillars, arches and a stucco-domed hall. What survives is only part of the original palace. In the evening the courtyard hosts a sound-and-light show on the king's life.
see: The Swargavilasam courtyard and its giant pillars
The evening sound-and-light show (check it is running)
thirumalai-nayakkar-mahal.best: Late afternoon, staying into the evening

gandhi-memorial-museum.why: In Madurai in 1921 Gandhi decided to wear only the simple loincloth of India's poor, a turning point in his life. The museum, in a 17th-century palace of Rani Mangammal, tells the story of the freedom struggle and keeps one of its most moving relics: the blood-stained cloth Gandhi wore when he was assassinated.
gandhi-memorial-museum.know: Parts of the museum have been under renovation; check before you go.

samanar-hills.why: Long before Madurai's great temples, Jain monks lived on these rock hills, sleeping on beds carved into the stone and leaving inscriptions in Tamil-Brahmi, one of the oldest scripts of the Tamil language. Later carvings of Jain teachers look out over a lotus pond. Climb up at dawn and watch the sun rise over paddy fields and the city.
see: The Jain stone beds and Tamil-Brahmi inscriptions
samanar-hills.know: No shade or shops at the top; carry water and wear good shoes.

keeladi-museum.hook: The town that rewrote Tamil history
keeladi-museum.why: Under coconut groves on the Vaigai, archaeologists found a brick-built Sangam-age town with streets, drains, ring wells, workshops, gold, dice, toys, and pottery scratched with Tamil-Brahmi letters. The state archaeology department dates its earliest layers to as early as the 6th century BCE, making it one of the strongest pieces of evidence for an early urban, literate Tamil society. The museum, in Chettinad-style buildings, tells the story beautifully.
see: Ring wells and the open-air excavation site, a kilometre away

pathu-thoon-ten-pillars.hook: Ten giant pillars of a vanished palace
pathu-thoon-ten-pillars.why: Hidden in a lane of textile shops behind the Nayakkar Mahal stand ten granite pillars about 12 metres tall. They are all that remains above ground of the Rangavilasam wing of Thirumalai Nayak's palace, where his brother is said to have lived. Most shoppers walk right past them: you won't, once you know.
see: The ten pillars, best looked at from the middle of the lane
The information board on the palace
The Nayakkar Mahal, a short walk away
pathu-thoon-ten-pillars.best: Morning, before the lane gets busy

alanganallur-jallikattu-vadivasal.hook: The gate the bulls burst through
alanganallur-jallikattu-vadivasal.why: Alanganallur's jallikattu is the most famous in Tamil Nadu. Every Pongal, more than a thousand bulls charge out of this vadivasal and tamers try to hang on to the hump for a few metres, while the whole village and visitors from around the world cheer from the galleries. Outside the season, you can stand at the gate and hear the stories from the villagers who raise the bulls.
see: The vadivasal gate and the galleries
Jallikattu itself in mid-January, during Pongal
alanganallur-jallikattu-vadivasal.spend: 1 hour; a full day on jallikattu day
alanganallur-jallikattu-vadivasal.know: On jallikattu day, watch only from the official galleries.

jallikattu-arena-alanganallur.hook: A stadium built for the bull-taming sport
jallikattu-arena-alanganallur.why: In 2024 the state opened this 67-acre arena near Alanganallur, below the hills, to host jallikattu with proper galleries and safety. It shows how seriously Tamil Nadu takes the sport as heritage. Outside the season you can walk the ground and imagine the roar.
see: The arena and galleries under the hills

mattuthavani-flower-market.hook: A mountain of jasmine before sunrise
mattuthavani-flower-market.why: Madurai malli, the city's GI-tagged jasmine, is traded here in heaps that perfume the whole street. Before dawn, farmers, garland-makers and traders bargain in a blur of white, orange and red. It is noisy, fragrant and one of the most photogenic sights in Madurai.

prema-vilas.hook: Hot halwa on a leaf, since 1954
prema-vilas.why: Madurai's day starts early, and so does Prema Vilas: from 4 am, wheat halwa glossy with ghee is scooped onto a leaf for you to eat on the spot. Locals buy it by the box to take home.
see: Mixture and other savouries to take away
prema-vilas.best: Early morning, when the halwa is freshest

aathi-kalathu-nei-mittai-kadai.hook: The original red-board sweet shop by the temple
aathi-kalathu-nei-mittai-kadai.why: Next to the temple, this is the shop with the red board: nei mittai, halwa, and a spicy kizhangu pottalam served until 1 pm. Small, old and loved by those who know.

murugan-idli-shop.why: Pillow-soft idli on a banana leaf with a row of chutneys and podi: the breakfast that made this shop a Madurai name.
see: Idli with the full chutney row

sulthan-hotel.hook: Mutton for breakfast, parotta past midnight
sulthan-hotel.why: A late-night institution: a mutton breakfast from 8 am, and parotta until 1 am for the city that doesn't sleep.

jaya-vilas.hook: A meals club hidden in a temple lane
jaya-vilas.why: Down a narrow lane near the temple, Jaya Vilas has served full meals since 1950. Ask for the ayirai fish curry and eat like a Madurai family.

hotel-sri-janakiram.why: A classic non-veg meals hall: rice on a banana leaf, three gravies poured in turn, and a mutton chukka worth the trip.

konar-kadai.hook: Where kari dosai is said to have been born
konar-kadai.why: Since 1943 this shop has been linked with Madurai's kari dosai: a thick dosai topped with egg and minced mutton. Order it, and you're eating a piece of city legend.

new-janani-mess.hook: Late-night mutton in the onion market
new-janani-mess.why: In the bustle of the onion market, this mess serves mutton chukka and vengaya kari until midnight.

p-power-hotel.hook: A long mutton menu for the adventurous
p-power-hotel.why: From brain roast to kari dosai, P. Power is where Madurai goes for every part of the goat, cooked hot.

muthukumar-bun-parotta.why: A ten-seat stall making the city's signature bun parotta, flaky and round, served with two salnas.

famous-jigarthanda.why: Milk, almond gum, nannari syrup and ice cream, layered in a glass: jigarthanda ('cool heart') is the drink Madurai is proud of, and this shop has served it since 1977.

thirumalai-madai-paruthi-paal.hook: Warm cottonseed milk, an old Madurai cure
thirumalai-madai-paruthi-paal.why: Paruthi paal is a rare drink of cottonseed milk with palm jaggery and dry ginger, sold warm in the evenings. Try something you won't find anywhere else.

kalapilla-tea-shop.hook: Butter bun and hot milk, the evening ritual
kalapilla-tea-shop.why: A tea shop of more than 50 years where the evening order is butter bun with hot cow's milk.

lakshmi-butter-bun-sellur.hook: Buns toasted in butter, eaten standing
lakshmi-butter-bun-sellur.why: A Sellur favourite: buns toasted in butter with sugar or palm jaggery, eaten on the pavement with the locals.

heritage-madurai.hook: Sleep among old trees in Tamil-style villas
heritage-madurai.why: Tamil-style rooms and villas in a green campus, with a pool shaped like a temple tank: a calm base after long temple days.

gateway-madurai-pasumalai.hook: A hilltop retreat with peacocks on the lawn
gateway-madurai-pasumalai.why: Colonial-style rooms on Pasumalai hill, with views over the city and peacocks wandering the gardens. Thiruparankundram is just down the road.

gopuram-grand.hook: Wake up facing the west gopuram
gopuram-grand.why: Steps from the temple: a simple, practical stay whose restaurant looks straight at Meenakshi's west tower.

east-masi-street-groceries.hook: The spice street of South Tamil Nadu
east-masi-street-groceries.why: Sacks of chillies, turmeric, dals and dry fruits spill out of wholesale shops where families stock up for weddings and festivals. Take home Madurai spices and podi.

south-masi-street-textiles.why: Multi-storey saree showrooms and old cloth wholesalers line the southern Masi street: silk for weddings, cotton for every day.

sungudi-sarees-munichalai.hook: Buy Madurai's own tie-dye saree from its makers
sungudi-sarees-munichalai.why: Sungudi is Madurai's GI-tagged tie-dye cotton, made by the city's Sourashtra weaving families with tiny dots tied by hand. Buying here supports the craft directly.

south-avani-moola-street-jewellery.hook: The gold street beside the temple
south-avani-moola-street-jewellery.why: Rows of jewellers selling temple-style necklaces, wedding sets and everyday gold, just south of Meenakshi.

valayalkara-street-bangles.hook: A street of bangles in every colour
valayalkara-street-bangles.why: Glass, metal, thread and bridal bangles stacked to the ceiling, wholesale and retail. A cheerful stop after temple darshan.

kamarajar-salai-vessels.why: Shops stacked with steel, brass and cast-iron cookware and lamps, where families buy wedding 'seer varisai' sets. Pick up a brass lamp or a cast-iron dosa pan to take home.

pudhu-mandapam.why: Facing the temple's east tower, this pillared hall from the Nayak period is carved with kings, gods and dancers, and was for generations a bazaar of tailors, brassware and books.
see: The east gopuram across the street
pudhu-mandapam.know: Its shops are moving to Kunnathur Chatram; check what's open.

central-vegetable-market.why: The old temple-area market, now on Melur Road: wholesale and retail vegetables, with the fruit and flower markets close by.

paravai-vegetable-market.hook: A market that comes alive at night
paravai-vegetable-market.why: One of south Tamil Nadu's biggest vegetable markets: lorries unload overnight and small eateries feed the night traders.

avaniyapuram-jallikattu.why: Every year Madurai's jallikattu season opens here, on the first day of Pongal. There is no stadium: the village's own street is double-barricaded and becomes the arena, and families crowd onto the terraces of their houses to watch the bulls and tamers charge past. It is raw, local and electric, and the closest of the three to the city.
see: Jallikattu on the first day of Pongal (mid-January)
Bulls being readied by their families before the run
avaniyapuram-jallikattu.best: Pongal day; be in place before sunrise
avaniyapuram-jallikattu.spend: Half a day on jallikattu day
avaniyapuram-jallikattu.know: Viewing space is limited and mostly on house terraces; follow police instructions and never enter the barricades.

palamedu-jallikattu-vadivasal.hook: Jallikattu on the day of the bulls
palamedu-jallikattu-vadivasal.why: On Mattu Pongal, the day Tamil Nadu honours its cattle, Palamedu opens its vadivasal and bull after bull charges into the arena while tamers try to hold the hump. Its galleries hold one of the biggest crowds of the season, and the village celebrates its bulls like heroes.
see: The vadivasal by the Bathrakaliyamman temple
palamedu-jallikattu-vadivasal.best: Mattu Pongal; arrive before dawn for a gallery seat
palamedu-jallikattu-vadivasal.spend: Half a day on jallikattu day
palamedu-jallikattu-vadivasal.know: Watch only from the galleries; the arena is for tamers and officials.

arittapatti-biodiversity-site.why: In 2022 Arittapatti became Tamil Nadu's first notified biodiversity heritage site, and it is easy to see why. Bare granite hills shelter more than 250 kinds of birds, including birds of prey that nest on the cliffs, along with the Anaikondan lake and Jain cave beds carved over two thousand years ago with Tamil-Brahmi inscriptions. It is wild, quiet and only half an hour from the city.
see: Birds of prey over the granite cliffs
Jain cave beds and Tamil-Brahmi inscriptions
arittapatti-biodiversity-site.best: Dawn, November to January for birds
arittapatti-biodiversity-site.know: No shops on the hills; carry water and go with a local guide if you can.
arittapatti-biodiversity-site.getting: By car or auto from Madurai, about 25 km by road, around an hour by car.

kutladampatti-falls.why: Locals call it Madurai's Kutralam: a waterfall in the Sirumalai foothills where families come to stand under the cascade after the rains. Through dry summers it can be a trickle, so time it right and it is a refreshing escape close to the city.
kutladampatti-falls.know: Visitors report it has been closed at times; check that it is open before you go.
kutladampatti-falls.getting: About 35 km by road, around an hour by car, via Vadipatti.

thiruvathavur-thirumarainathar-temple.hook: Birthplace of the poet who sang Thiruvasagam
thiruvathavur-thirumarainathar-temple.why: Manikkavasagar, whose Thiruvasagam is among the most loved Tamil devotional poems, was born here. The Shiva temple is a calm, pure example of Pandya stone architecture with many holy tanks, and a short, easy trip from Madurai into the countryside.
thiruvathavur-thirumarainathar-temple.getting: City buses 66 and 66J from Periyar and Arappalayam via Mattuthavani, or by car, about 30 km by road, around an hour by car.

dindigul-rock-fort.hook: A fort on one giant rock
dindigul-rock-fort.why: The Madurai Nayaks built this fort on a single massive rock in the 17th century. Hyder Ali and Tipu Sultan later held it, and then the British. Climb the steps cut into the rock to a breezy top with views over Dindigul and the Sirumalai hills, then reward yourself with Dindigul's famous biryani.
see: The fort walls and cannon points
dindigul-rock-fort.best: Early morning or late afternoon; the rock gets hot
dindigul-rock-fort.getting: Buses to Dindigul leave from Arappalayam bus stand; trains run from Madurai Junction. About 65 km by road, around 1.5 hours by car.

sirumalai-hills.why: Eighteen hairpin bends lift you out of the heat into forest, mist and fresh air. Sirumalai is a quiet, uncommercial hill range with a viewpoint tower over Dindigul and the plains, small temples, and the famous Sirumalai hill banana.
sirumalai-hills.know: Pay the vehicle entry fee at the forest check post; drive carefully on the bends.
sirumalai-hills.getting: Via Dindigul, about 50 km by road, around an hour by car.

srivilliputhur-andal-temple.hook: The tower on Tamil Nadu's emblem
srivilliputhur-andal-temple.why: This is the birthplace of Andal, the only woman among the twelve Alvar saints, who wrote the Thiruppavai and is worshipped here as the bride of Vishnu. Its towering rajagopuram is the emblem of the Government of Tamil Nadu. Finish with Srivilliputhur's famous palkova, a sweet made from slow-cooked milk.
see: The rajagopuram on the state emblem
Andal's shrine and the Vadapathrasayi temple
srivilliputhur-andal-temple.know: Phones are kept in lockers outside.
srivilliputhur-andal-temple.getting: About 90 km by road, around 2 hours by car.

pillayarpatti-karpaga-vinayagar-temple.hook: Ganesha carved into rock in Chettinad
pillayarpatti-karpaga-vinayagar-temple.why: One of the oldest rock-cut Ganesha shrines in India, carved into a hillock and cared for by Chettinad's Nagarathar community. Devotees come from around the world to pray to Karpaga Vinayagar, the wish-granting Ganesha, before any new beginning.
pillayarpatti-karpaga-vinayagar-temple.getting: About 85 km by road, around 2 hours by car; combine with Chettinad.

kundrakudi-murugan-temple.why: About 150 rock-cut steps lead up to Murugan with six faces, seated on his peacock with Valli and Deivanai. The view from the top over Chettinad's countryside is a bonus, and Pillayarpatti is just down the road.
kundrakudi-murugan-temple.getting: About 85 km by road, around 2 hours by car; near Pillayarpatti.

kanadukathan-chettinad-palace.why: A century ago the Nagarathar merchants of Chettinad traded across Southeast Asia and came home to build palaces: Burma teak pillars, Italian marble, Belgian glass and handmade Athangudi tiles. Kanadukathan's streets are lined with these mansions. Walk them, step into the ones open to visitors, and end with a Chettinad meal.
see: Mansions open for a fee, such as A R House
kanadukathan-chettinad-palace.know: Many mansions are private homes; some open for a small fee. Be respectful.
kanadukathan-chettinad-palace.getting: About 100 km by road, around 2 hours by car.

athangudi-tiles.hook: Tiles made by hand, one at a time
athangudi-tiles.why: Chettinad's colourful Athangudi tiles are made with no kiln: patterns are poured into moulds by hand on glass and left to cure. At the workshops you can watch every step and take home a tile or two.
athangudi-tiles.best: Weekday daytime, when the workers are busy
athangudi-tiles.getting: About 95 km by road, around 2 hours by car; near Karaikudi.

thirumayam-fort.hook: Boulders, cannons and a hilltop view
thirumayam-fort.why: Built in 1687, this fort climbs a hill of giant boulders, with cannons still on the ramparts, a Shiva shrine cut into the rock and a sweeping view over the plains toward Chettinad. A good stop on the road through Chettinad.
thirumayam-fort.know: Little shade; carry water and a hat.
thirumayam-fort.getting: About 100 km by road, around 2.5 hours by car; on the Karaikudi–Pudukkottai road.

vaigai-dam.hook: Where Madurai's river is held back
vaigai-dam.why: The Vaigai, Madurai's river, is stored here in the shadow of the Western Ghats. The gardens below the dam make a breezy family picnic, with a children's park and walks along the bund.
vaigai-dam.getting: Buses to Theni and Andipatti leave from Arappalayam bus stand. About 80 km by road, around 1.5 hours by car.

kumbakkarai-falls.hook: A forest bath at the foot of Kodaikanal
kumbakkarai-falls.why: Water from the Kodaikanal hills tumbles over rocks into natural pools here. It is a favourite place to bathe and cool off, among forest, butterflies and a few cheeky monkeys.
kumbakkarai-falls.know: Carry cash for entry and parking; keep food away from monkeys.
kumbakkarai-falls.getting: Buses to Theni and Periyakulam leave from Arappalayam bus stand. About 90 km by road, around 2 hours by car.

sathuragiri-hills.hook: A pilgrim's trek to the Siddhars' mountain
sathuragiri-hills.why: Deep in the Western Ghats, Sathuragiri is believed to be the home of the 18 Siddhars. Pilgrims climb an 8 km forest path from Thaniparai to the Sundara Mahalingam temple, sharing food and stories on the way.
see: Sundara Mahalingam and Santhana Mahalingam shrines
sathuragiri-hills.best: The permitted days around new moon and full moon
sathuragiri-hills.know: Access is allowed only on set days; check with the forest department. Wear good shoes and carry water.
sathuragiri-hills.getting: To Thaniparai, about 70 km by road, around 1.5 hours by car.

vettangudi-bird-sanctuary.why: Every winter, village tanks at Vettangudi fill with nesting painted storks, herons, egrets and migrants from far away. Watch them from the towers and the bund path.
vettangudi-bird-sanctuary.know: Bring binoculars; there are few facilities.
vettangudi-bird-sanctuary.getting: About 60 km by road, around 1.5 hours by car; near Tiruppattur.

thiruchuli-thirumeninathar-temple.why: A great old Shiva temple praised in the Devaram hymns, beside the Gundar river. A few steps away is the house where Ramana Maharshi was born, now a quiet meditation hall.
thiruchuli-thirumeninathar-temple.getting: About 55 km by road, around 1.5 hours by car; via Aruppukottai.

kalayarkoil-temple.hook: The temple of the Marudhu brothers
kalayarkoil-temple.why: Three Shiva shrines stand within one temple here, under a towering gopuram. It is bound up with the Marudhu brothers of Sivaganga, who fought the British at the turn of the 19th century and rebuilt the temple.
kalayarkoil-temple.getting: About 75 km by road, around 1.5 hours by car; via Sivaganga.

sivaganga-palace.hook: The palace of Queen Velu Nachiyar's kingdom
sivaganga-palace.why: Gowri Vilasam palace was the seat of the Sivaganga kingdom, the land of Queen Velu Nachiyar, who fought the East India Company in the 1780s, and of the Marudhu brothers. The descendants of the royal family still live here.
see: Navaratri, when it opens in the evenings
sivaganga-palace.know: Closed on Sundays; parts are a private residence.
sivaganga-palace.getting: About 55 km by road, around an hour by car.
